In light of these considerations, what then is the analytical difference 
between the ChevroTt and Loper Bright frameworks? Consider the cases 
previously decided under ''Chevrorb Step 1” (where Congress has “directly 
spoken to the precise issue”). Presumably, such cases come out the same under 
both frameworks. Consider, next, cases using language like “reasonable” or 
“appropriate.” Such cases were State Farm cases prior to Loper Bright, and 
remain State Farm cases under Loper Bright. The last set of cases are those 
categorized under “Chevrorb Step 2,” where there might be a “best” 
interpretation of the statute, but there are reasonable, permissible 
alternatives. According to Loper Bright, those cases are for the court to decide, 
whereas Chevrorb would have allocated interpretive authority to the agency.
Exactly how many cases fall in this category is difficult to quantify with 
precision. But it appears that this describes the manner in which Loper Bright 
practically changed the interpretive framework that previously existed under 
Chevrorb. See Aditya Bamzai, Judicial Defererbce arbd Doctrirbal Clarity, 82 
Oh io  St . L.J. 585 (2021).
5. 
Empirical Studies. Of course, at the time of this writing, no empirical 
work has been done on the significance of the Loper Bright Court’s overruling 
of Chevrorb. But during the Chevrorb era, several studies sought to cast hght on 
the question whether the Court’s articulation of a deference standard affected 
the outcomes of cases.
Professor Eskridge and his coauthor Lauren Baer conducted a large study 
of all Supreme Court cases decided between the 1983 term and the 2005 term 
of the Supreme Court in which federal agency interpretation of a statute was 
at issue—1,014 cases in all. William N. Eskridge, Jr. & Lauren E. Baer, The 
Corbtirbuum of Defererbce: Supreme Court Treatmerbt of Agerbcy Statutory 
Irbterpretatiorbs From Chevron to Hamdan, 96 Ge o . L.J. 1083 (2008). The article 
canvassed most of the major doctrinal issues that surrounded the appHcation 
of Chevrorb. According to the authors:
Based upon our data, we conclude that there has not been a 
Chevrorb “revolution” at the Supreme Court level. The deference 
regime associated with the Chevrorb decision is not completely new 
and continues to exist alongside old feudal lords—Skidmore, 
Semirbole Rock, Curtiss-Wright, and Beth Israel. Indeed, from the 
time it was handed down until the end of the 2005 term, Chevrorb was 
applied in only 8.3% of Supreme Court cases evaluating agency 
statutory interpretations * * *.  During this time frame, the Court 
employed a continuum of deference regimes. This continuum is more 
complicated than the hterature or even the Court’s own opinions 
suggest, and it is a continuum in which Chevrorb plays a modest role. 
Indeed, our most striking finding is that in the majority of cases— 
53.6% of them—^the Court does not apply any deference regime at all. 
Instead, it rehes on ad hoc judicial reasoning of the sort that typifies 
the Court’s methodology in regular statutory interpretation cases.
